figs.title: Fibre kinking: compressive strength versus misalignment
figs.caption: In compression each fibre is a slender column braced by the soft matrix. Misaligned fibres rotate, the matrix yields in shear, and a kink band forms at σ_c = τ_y/(γ_y + φ), which starts at G₁₂ for perfect alignment and is already halved when φ equals γ_y (0.69° here).

figs.title: Transversely isotropic compliance matrix
figs.caption: With the fibre along axis 1 and an isotropic 2-3 plane, the compliance matrix holds five independent constants: E₁, ν₁₂, G₁₂, E₂ and ν₂₃. The transverse shear term follows from the plane's isotropy, 1/G₂₃ = 2(1 + ν₂₃)/E₂.

figs.title: Hole edge stress under biaxial loads
figs.caption: Superposing two Kirsch solutions gives the edge hoop stress σ_θθ = (σ₁ + σ₂) − 2(σ₁ − σ₂)cos 2θ. The peak 3σ₁ − σ₂ is 3σ₁ in uniaxial tension, 2.5σ₁ in a pressurised cylinder skin, 2σ₁ for equibiaxial tension and 4σ₁ in pure shear.

figs.title: Hot bore thick cylinder: thermal stress through the wall
figs.caption: Steady conduction makes T vary with ln r. The hot bore wants to grow and the cooler outer layers hold it back, so the hoop stress is compressive at the bore and tensile at the outside, while σ_rr vanishes at both faces.

figs.title: Mooney-Rivlin balloon: peak, valley and rising branch
figs.caption: The geometric factor λ⁻¹ − λ⁻⁷ falls after the peak, and the factor C₁ + C₂λ² brings the pressure back up at large stretch. Under slowly rising pressure the balloon snaps from the peak to the rising branch at the same pressure.
